concept: Section 61.129 is the aeronautical experience rule for the commercial certificate
q: Which regulation sets the aeronautical experience for a commercial certificate, and what is its official title?
a: 14 CFR 61.129, Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), officially titled 'Aeronautical experience.' In plain English it lists the hours and the specific flights you must have logged before you may take the commercial practical test; paragraph (a) is the airplane single-engine land list. It works alongside 61.123 eligibility, 61.125 knowledge areas and 61.127 areas of operation. Part 141 students meet a reduced total instead.

concept: 250 hours of total flight time
q: How much total flight time does 61.129(a) require for a commercial airplane single-engine certificate?
a: 250 hours of total time as a pilot under 61.129(a), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' That total must contain at least 100 hours in powered aircraft, at least 100 hours of pilot-in-command time, the solo or duties-of-PIC flights, the 20 hours of commercial training, and the day and night cross-countries. An approved Part 141 course requires 190 hours instead, so know which rule you are training under.

concept: At least 100 hours in powered aircraft
q: Of the 250 hours, how many must be in powered aircraft?
a: At least 100 hours in powered aircraft under 61.129(a)(1), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Powered aircraft means anything other than a glider or balloon, so helicopter, powered-lift and airplane time all count toward this 100; the remaining 150 hours of the 250 may come from any pilot time, including glider or balloon time.

concept: 50 of the 100 powered hours must be in airplanes
q: How much of the 100 hours in powered aircraft must be in airplanes?
a: At least 50 hours in airplanes, under 61.129(a)(1), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' So of the 100 powered hours, half must be airplane time; the balance may be in other powered categories. A Warrior II flight counts toward both the powered-aircraft 100 and the airplane 50.

concept: At least 100 hours pilot-in-command
q: How many hours of pilot-in-command time does the commercial certificate require?
a: At least 100 hours of pilot-in-command time under 61.129(a)(2), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' PIC here is logged under 61.51(e), which includes time as sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft for which you are rated, so dual received in your Warrior II as a rated private pilot is loggable PIC toward this 100.

concept: At least 50 of the PIC hours in airplanes
q: Of the 100 hours pilot-in-command, how many must be in airplanes?
a: At least 50 hours of the pilot-in-command time must be in airplanes, per 61.129(a)(2)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The other 50 PIC hours may be in any other powered category or class you are rated for.

concept: At least 50 hours PIC cross-country
q: How much cross-country pilot-in-command time is required for the commercial certificate?
a: At least 50 hours of cross-country flight time as pilot in command, per 61.129(a)(2)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' For this purpose cross-country under 61.1 means a landing at a point more than 50 nautical miles straight-line from the original point of departure, with the usual landing, navigation and planning elements.

concept: 10 of the 50 cross-country hours must be in airplanes
q: How much of the 50 hours of cross-country PIC time must be in airplanes?
a: At least 10 of the 50 cross-country PIC hours must be in airplanes, per 61.129(a)(2)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The other 40 may be in any other powered category or class. In practice a private pilot building commercial time in a Warrior II will far exceed the 10.

concept: 10 hours solo in a single-engine airplane, or 10 hours performing the duties of PIC with an instructor on board
q: What are the two ways to satisfy the 10-hour solo requirement under 61.129(a)(4)?
a: Either 10 hours of solo flight time in a single-engine airplane, or 10 hours of flight time performing the duties of pilot in command in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor on board, under 61.129(a)(4), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' You must pick one path and complete all its required flights the same way; the two cannot be mixed within those flights.

concept: One cross-country of not less than 300 NM total distance with landings at a minimum of 3 points
q: Describe the long cross-country required by 61.129(a)(4)(i).
a: One cross-country flight of not less than 300 nautical miles total distance, with landings at a minimum of three points, flown solo or performing the duties of pilot in command with an instructor aboard, per 61.129(a)(4)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Total distance is the sum of the legs; three points means three landings, which with the departure airport is a four-airport route or a route returning home.

concept: One leg of the 300 NM cross-country a straight-line distance of at least 250 NM from the original departure point
q: On the 300 NM commercial cross-country, what is the 250 NM requirement exactly?
a: One of the landing points must be a straight-line distance of at least 250 nautical miles from the original departure point, per 61.129(a)(4)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The 250 is measured from the original point of departure to that landing point, not leg to leg, so plan the route to prove the straight-line distance on the chart or a flight planning log.

concept: Special circumstances with Hawaii on the long cross-country
q: How does the 300 NM commercial cross-country requirement change if it is flown in Hawaii?
a: If the flight is conducted in Hawaii, the longest segment need only have a straight-line distance of at least 150 nautical miles, per 61.129(a)(4)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' The rest of the requirement stands: not less than 300 nautical miles total distance with landings at a minimum of three points.

concept: 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings
q: What night flying is required by 61.129(a)(4)(ii) for the commercial certificate?
a: 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings, flown solo or performing the duties of pilot in command with an instructor aboard, per 61.129(a)(4)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Night here is the 61.1 definition: the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight.

concept: Each of the 10 night landings must involve a flight in the traffic pattern at an airport with an operating control tower
q: What two conditions attach to the 10 night takeoffs and landings for the commercial certificate?
a: Each landing must involve a flight in the traffic pattern, and they must be at an airport with an operating control tower, per 61.129(a)(4)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Touch and goes count so long as each is preceded by a circuit of the pattern; the tower must actually be operating at the time, so a tower that closes at 2200 local stops counting then.

concept: At least 20 hours of training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127(b)(1)
q: How many hours of training on the commercial areas of operation does 61.129(a)(3) require?
a: At least 20 hours of training from an authorized instructor on the areas of operation listed in 61.127(b)(1), per 61.129(a)(3), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Those 20 hours must themselves contain the 10 hours of instrument training, the 10 hours in a complex, turbine-powered or technically advanced airplane, the two 2-hour cross-countries, and the 3 hours of practical test preparation.

concept: At least 10 hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device
q: How much instrument training does the commercial certificate require, and how much of it must be in an airplane?
a: At least 10 hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device, of which at least 5 hours must be in a single-engine airplane, per 61.129(a)(3)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Up to 5 hours may be credited from an approved full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device under 61.129(i).

concept: Content of the instrument training: attitude instrument flying, partial panel, unusual attitude recovery, intercepting and tracking navigational systems
q: What four subjects must the 10 hours of commercial instrument training cover?
a: Attitude instrument flying, partial panel skills, recovery from unusual flight attitudes, and intercepting and tracking navigational systems, per 61.129(a)(3)(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' In the Warrior II partial panel usually means losing the vacuum-driven attitude indicator and directional gyro and flying on the turn coordinator, magnetic compass, altimeter and airspeed indicator; confirm the panel fit against the POH.

concept: One 2-hour day cross-country with a total straight-line distance of more than 100 NM
q: Describe the day cross-country required within the 20 hours of commercial training.
a: One 2-hour cross-country flight in daytime conditions in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor, consisting of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure, per 61.129(a)(3)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' It is dual training time, not solo, and the 2 hours is flight time, not block time.

concept: One 2-hour night cross-country with a total straight-line distance of more than 100 NM
q: Describe the night cross-country required within the 20 hours of commercial training.
a: One 2-hour cross-country flight in nighttime conditions in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor, consisting of a total straight-line distance of more than 100 nautical miles from the original point of departure, per 61.129(a)(3)(iii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' It is separate from the day flight and from the 5 hours of night VFR solo or duties-of-PIC time.

concept: At least 3 hours with an authorized instructor in a single-engine airplane in preparation for the practical test within the preceding 2 calendar months
q: What is the 3-hour practical test preparation requirement, and how recent must it be?
a: At least 3 hours in a single-engine airplane with an authorized instructor in preparation for the practical test, completed within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test, per 61.129(a)(3)(iv), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' Calendar months means it expires at the end of the second month, so training in March is good for a test through the end of May.

concept: At least 10 hours of training in a complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane, or a technically advanced airplane (TAA)
q: What are your three options for the 10 hours of complex or advanced airplane training?
a: A complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane, or a technically advanced airplane (TAA), per 61.129(a)(3)(ii), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Aeronautical experience.' A TAA under 61.129(j) has an electronically advanced avionics system with a primary flight display, a multifunction display including a moving map, and a two-axis autopilot. A stock 1981 Warrior II is none of the three, so this time is flown in a different airplane.
dup: What is a technically advanced airplane?

concept: Note: an instrument rating alone does not satisfy the commercial training requirements
q: Does holding an instrument rating satisfy the training required for a commercial certificate?
a: No. The instrument rating is a separate certificate action; 61.129(a)(3) still requires 20 hours of training on the 61.127(b)(1) commercial areas of operation, including the 10 hours of instrument training with a view-limiting device, the two 2-hour cross-countries, and the 3 hours of practical test preparation. Whether any earlier instrument training may be credited toward the 10 hours is an endorsement decision for your instructor; check 61.129(a)(3)(i) and current FAA legal interpretations.

concept: Section 61.127(b)(1) areas of operation for the commercial single-engine airplane
q: What is 61.127(b)(1), and why does it matter to your commercial training?
a: 14 CFR 61.127, Part 61, Subpart F, is titled 'Flight proficiency,' and paragraph (b)(1) lists the areas of operation for an airplane single-engine rating: preflight preparation; preflight procedures; airport and seaplane base operations; takeoffs, landings and go-arounds; performance maneuvers; ground reference maneuvers; navigation; slow flight and stalls; emergency operations; high-altitude operations; and postflight procedures. The 20 hours of commercial training and the practical test are both built on this list.

concept: Section 61.123 is the eligibility rule for the commercial pilot certificate
q: Which regulation lists eligibility for a commercial pilot certificate, and what is its official title?
a: 14 CFR 61.123, Part 61, Subpart F (Commercial Pilots), titled 'Eligibility requirements: General.' In plain English it is the checklist of who may be issued the certificate: age, English, the ground and flight training endorsements, the knowledge test, the aeronautical experience of 61.129, the practical test, and holding at least a private pilot certificate.

concept: At least 18 years of age
q: What is the minimum age for a commercial pilot certificate?
a: 18 years of age, per 61.123(a), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' You may take the knowledge test before turning 18, and you may hold a private certificate at 17, but the commercial certificate itself cannot be issued until your eighteenth birthday.

concept: Be able to read, speak, write, and understand English
q: What is the English language requirement for a commercial certificate?
a: You must be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language, per 61.123(b), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' If a medical condition limits any of those abilities, the FAA may place an operating limitation on the certificate as needed for safety.

concept: Logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the ground training or reviewed the home study on the 61.125 knowledge areas
q: What endorsement must you hold before taking the commercial knowledge test?
a: A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who either conducted the required ground training or reviewed your home study on the aeronautical knowledge areas of 61.125, per 61.123(c), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' Home study counts only if an instructor has reviewed it and signs for it.

concept: The instructor must certify that the person is prepared for the required knowledge test
q: What exactly must the instructor certify in the knowledge test endorsement?
a: That you are prepared for the required knowledge test, per 61.123(c)(2), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The endorsement is a statement of readiness, not merely of attendance, and the testing center will not let you sit the test without it. Wording is in the current AC 61-65 endorsement guide.

concept: Pass the required knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in 61.125
q: What knowledge test must a commercial applicant pass, and what does it cover?
a: The commercial pilot knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas of 61.125, required by 61.123(d), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The passing score is 70 percent, and the test report is valid for 24 calendar months from the month it was taken, so the practical test must be completed within that window.

concept: Section 61.125 aeronautical knowledge areas
q: What is 61.125, and what sort of subjects does it list?
a: 14 CFR 61.125, Part 61, Subpart F, titled 'Aeronautical knowledge,' lists the ground subjects a commercial applicant must learn: the regulations relating to commercial privileges and limitations; accident reporting under NTSB 830; basic aerodynamics and principles of flight; meteorology and weather reports; safe and efficient operation; weight and balance; performance charts; night and high-altitude operations; and aeronautical decision making and judgment.

concept: Receive the required training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127
q: What endorsement must you hold before the commercial practical test?
a: A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who conducted the training on the areas of operation listed in 61.127, per 61.123(e), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' That instructor must also have given or verified the 3 hours of test preparation within the preceding 2 calendar months required by 61.129(a)(3)(iv).

concept: The instructor must certify that the person is prepared for the required practical test
q: What must the practical test endorsement say about your readiness?
a: It must certify that you are prepared for the required practical test, per 61.123(e)(2), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The examiner checks this endorsement, the knowledge test report, your logbook experience and your aircraft paperwork before the test begins. Endorsement wording comes from the current AC 61-65.

concept: Section 61.127 areas of operation
q: What is 61.127, and how is it used on the commercial checkride?
a: 14 CFR 61.127, Part 61, Subpart F, titled 'Flight proficiency,' lists the areas of operation you must be trained in and tested on. For an airplane single-engine rating under (b)(1) that is preflight preparation; preflight procedures; airport operations; takeoffs, landings and go-arounds; performance maneuvers; ground reference maneuvers; navigation; slow flight and stalls; emergency operations; high-altitude operations; and postflight procedures. The Airman Certification Standards expand each one into tasks.

concept: Meet the aeronautical experience requirements of this subpart that apply to the aircraft category and class rating
q: Which experience must a commercial applicant meet, and does it depend on the aircraft?
a: You must meet the aeronautical experience requirements of 61.129 that apply to the category and class rating sought, per 61.123(f), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' The hours differ by category and class: 61.129(a) is airplane single-engine land, (b) is multiengine, (c) and (d) are rotorcraft, and so on.

concept: Pass the required practical test on the areas of operation listed in 61.127
q: What practical test must a commercial applicant pass?
a: The commercial pilot practical test on the areas of operation listed in 61.127 for the category and class sought, per 61.123(g), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' It is conducted to the Commercial Pilot Airman Certification Standards and includes both an oral and a flight portion; the airplane you bring must meet 61.45, which for the single-engine commercial means an airplane capable of performing all required tasks.

concept: Hold at least a private pilot certificate issued under this part or meet the requirements of 61.73
q: Must you already be a private pilot to be issued a commercial certificate?
a: Yes. You must hold at least a private pilot certificate issued under Part 61, or meet the requirements of 61.73, per 61.123(h), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' There is no route straight from student pilot to commercial pilot; the private certificate, or its military equivalent processed under 61.73, is the entry ticket.

concept: Section 61.73 as the alternative to holding a Part 61 private certificate
q: What is 61.73, and who uses it on the way to a commercial certificate?
a: 14 CFR 61.73, Part 61, Subpart A (General), titled 'Military pilots or former military pilots: Special rules.' It lets a qualified United States military pilot obtain a civil pilot certificate and ratings on the basis of military qualification rather than by taking the normal private pilot course, and that certificate then satisfies the private pilot prerequisite in 61.123(h).

concept: Comply with the sections of this part that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought
q: What is the catch-all eligibility item at the end of 61.123?
a: You must comply with the sections of Part 61 that apply to the aircraft category and class rating sought, per 61.123(i), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Eligibility requirements: General.' That sweeps in items such as 61.31 endorsements for the airplane used, 61.39 prerequisites for the practical test, and 61.23 medical certificate requirements.

concept: Tailwheel endorsement 61.31(i)
q: What does 61.31(i) require before you act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane?
a: Ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane, and a one-time logbook endorsement certifying proficiency, per 61.31(i), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements.' A pilot who logged pilot-in-command time in a tailwheel airplane before April 15, 1991 is not required to have the endorsement.
dup: What must you do before acting as PIC of a tailwheel airplane?

concept: Tailwheel endorsement does not require a minimum number of hours
q: How many hours of training does the tailwheel endorsement require?
a: No minimum number of hours. 61.31(i), Part 61, Subpart A, specifies the maneuvers that must be trained, not a time; the instructor signs when you are proficient. In practice it runs five to ten hours, but the regulation sets no floor.

concept: Tailwheel maneuvers required: normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings, go-around procedures
q: Which specific maneuvers must the tailwheel training cover?
a: Normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings, and go-around procedures, per 61.31(i)(1), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements.' Wheel landings may be omitted only if the manufacturer has recommended against them for that airplane.

concept: Tailwheel grandfather provision for pilots who logged PIC tailwheel time before April 15, 1991
q: Is there any exception to the tailwheel endorsement requirement?
a: Yes. A pilot who logged pilot-in-command time in a tailwheel airplane before April 15, 1991 is excepted, per 61.31(i)(2), Part 61, Subpart A. Nobody earning a certificate today can use that exception, and insurance will usually demand training and a checkout regardless of what the regulation allows.

concept: Complex endorsement 61.31(e) and the definition of a complex airplane
q: What makes an airplane complex, and what must you have to act as PIC of one?
a: A complex airplane has retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller, including an airplane with a FADEC engine and propeller control system; a seaplane needs only flaps and a controllable pitch propeller. You must receive and log ground and flight training from an authorized instructor and hold a one-time logbook endorsement, per 61.31(e), Part 61, Subpart A. Your fixed-gear, fixed-pitch Warrior II is not complex.
dup: What makes an airplane complex, and what is required to fly one as PIC?

concept: Complex endorsement does not require a minimum number of hours
q: Is there a minimum number of hours for the complex endorsement?
a: No minimum hours are specified in 61.31(e), Part 61, Subpart A. The instructor trains you to proficiency in that make and model and then endorses your logbook. Note that the commercial certificate separately requires 10 hours of training in a complex, turbine-powered or technically advanced airplane under 61.129(a)(3)(ii), which is a different requirement.

concept: Complex endorsement requires logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor
q: What form does complex training have to take before the endorsement is signed?
a: You must receive and log both ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a complex airplane, or in an approved full flight simulator or flight training device representing one, and be found proficient in its operation, per 61.31(e)(1), Part 61, Subpart A. The instructor then makes the one-time logbook endorsement under 61.31(e)(2).

concept: High performance endorsement 61.31(f): more than 200 horsepower
q: What is a high performance airplane, and what is required before you fly one as PIC?
a: An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower. You must receive and log ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a high performance airplane, or an approved simulator or flight training device, be found proficient, and hold a one-time logbook endorsement, per 61.31(f), Part 61, Subpart A. A Warrior II has a 160 horsepower Lycoming O-320, so it is not high performance; confirm the installed engine against the POH.
dup: What is a high performance airplane, and what is required to act as PIC of one?

concept: High performance endorsement requires logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor
q: Does the high performance endorsement have an hour requirement?
a: No minimum hours are specified in 61.31(f), Part 61, Subpart A. What is required is logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor and a finding of proficiency, followed by the one-time logbook endorsement. Exactly 200 horsepower is not high performance; the rule says more than 200.

concept: High altitude endorsement 61.31(g): pressurized airplane with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 ft MSL
q: Which airplanes require a high altitude endorsement?
a: A pressurized airplane with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL, per 61.31(g), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements.' The test is the airplane's certificated capability, not the altitude you intend to fly; an unpressurized airplane never needs it, so your Warrior II does not.
dup: What is a high altitude airplane, and what training does the endorsement require?

concept: High altitude endorsement requires logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor
q: What two kinds of training does the high altitude endorsement require?
a: Both ground training and flight training, received and logged from an authorized instructor in a pressurized airplane or in an approved simulator or flight training device, followed by a finding of proficiency and a one-time logbook endorsement, per 61.31(g)(1) and (g)(2), Part 61, Subpart A. There is no minimum hour requirement. A pilot who logged PIC time in such an airplane before April 15, 1991, or who passed an equivalent FAA or military proficiency check, is excepted.

concept: High altitude ground training subject list
q: List the subjects the high altitude ground training must cover.
a: High-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology; respiration; hypoxia and other high-altitude sicknesses; duration of consciousness without supplemental oxygen; effects of prolonged use of supplemental oxygen; causes and effects of gas expansion and gas bubble formation, and how to prevent them; physical phenomena and incidents of decompression; and any other physiological aspects of high-altitude flight, per 61.31(g)(1)(i), Part 61, Subpart A.

concept: High altitude flight training content
q: What must the flight portion of high altitude training include?
a: Normal cruise flight operations above 25,000 feet MSL; proper emergency procedures for a simulated rapid decompression, without actually depressurizing the aircraft; and emergency descent procedures, per 61.31(g)(1)(ii), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements.'

concept: The four endorsements are one-time and do not expire
q: Do the tailwheel, complex, high performance and high altitude endorsements expire?
a: No, all four are one-time endorsements that never expire and are not make-and-model specific under 61.31, Part 61, Subpart A. They are also not currency items, so no recurring flight is required to keep them. Insurance requirements and good judgment are separate matters, and a flight review under 61.56 is still needed every 24 calendar months.
dup: Do the high performance, high altitude, tailwheel and complex endorsements ever expire?

concept: Which of the four endorsements apply to a 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II
q: Which of the four 61.31 endorsements does your Warrior II require?
a: None of them. A 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II has fixed tricycle gear, a fixed-pitch propeller, a 160 horsepower carbureted Lycoming O-320, and no pressurization, so it is not complex under 61.31(e), not high performance under 61.31(f), not a high altitude airplane under 61.31(g), and not a tailwheel airplane under 61.31(i). Confirm the engine and propeller fitted to your serial number against the POH and the aircraft records.

concept: 61.51(g)(1) definition of loggable instrument time
q: Under 61.51(g)(1), what flight time may be logged as instrument time?
a: Only that flight time during which the person operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments under actual or simulated instrument flight conditions, per 61.51(g)(1), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' It is time spent on the gauges, not time spent on an IFR flight plan; cruising on top in clear air on an IFR clearance is not instrument time.
dup: Under 61.51, what makes flight time loggable as instrument time?

concept: 61.51(g)(2) instructor logging instrument time in actual conditions
q: When may an instructor log instrument time while teaching?
a: An authorized instructor may log instrument time when conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument flight conditions, per 61.51(g)(2), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' The instructor cannot log instrument time for simulated instrument instruction given in visual conditions, although the student under the hood can.

concept: 61.51(g)(3) logbook entry: location and type of each instrument approach
q: What must you record in your logbook for each instrument approach flown?
a: The location and type of each instrument approach accomplished, per 61.51(g)(3)(i), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' Location means the airport identifier and type means the kind of approach, for example 'KLNS ILS 08' or 'KMDT RNAV (GPS) 31'. This is how you prove the six approaches required for instrument currency under 61.57(c).
dup: What must your logbook show for each instrument approach and for simulated instrument time?

concept: 61.51(g)(3) logbook entry: name of the safety pilot
q: When logging simulated instrument time, whose name goes in the logbook, and who may serve in that seat?
a: The name of the safety pilot, if one is required, per 61.51(g)(3)(ii), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' Under 91.109(c) the safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft, have adequate vision forward and to each side, and the aircraft must have dual controls, or an approved observation seat and visibility arrangement.
dup: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?

concept: 61.51(g)(4) logging instrument time in a flight simulator, flight training device or ATD
q: May instrument time be logged in a simulator or training device, and how is it recorded?
a: Yes, in an approved full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device, per 61.51(g)(4), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' The entry must identify the device used and the time, and must be distinguished from aircraft time. 61.57(c) sets how much instrument currency may be regained in each type of device.
dup: Can instrument currency be regained in a simulator or training device?

concept: Simulator time used for a certificate or rating requires the instructor's name and certificate number
q: If simulator instrument time is used toward a certificate or rating, what extra entry is required?
a: The name and certificate number of the authorized instructor who provided the training must be entered, per 61.51(g)(4), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Pilot logbooks.' Training credited toward a certificate or rating must be given by an authorized instructor present with you at the device, and the instructor signs the logbook.

concept: Simulator time used only for currency by an instrument rated pilot needs no instructor
q: Do you need an instructor to use a training device purely for instrument currency?
a: For an instrument-rated pilot regaining or maintaining currency, no instructor is required in an approved aviation training device under 61.57(c), although an instructor or an authorized person may be needed to observe or sign depending on the device. Record the device, the date, the tasks, the approaches, holding and course intercepting and tracking. Confirm the current wording of 61.57(c) and any letter of authorization for the specific device.

concept: Safety pilot qualification requirements under 91.109
q: What does 91.109 require of the airplane and the safety pilot for simulated instrument flight?
a: 14 CFR 91.109, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Flight instruction; simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests,' requires fully functioning dual controls and a safety pilot who holds at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft and has adequate vision forward and to each side. The safety pilot must also hold a medical certificate or BasicMed because that pilot is a required crewmember.

concept: Instrument rating required to act as PIC in IFR weather conditions
q: When does 61.3 require you to hold an instrument rating?
a: To act as pilot in command of a civil aircraft under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR flight, per 61.3(e), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations.' You must hold the instrument rating on your certificate for the category of aircraft flown and be current under 61.57(c).

concept: 61.133 commercial limitation: no instrument rating means no passengers for hire on cross-countries over 50 NM or at night
q: What limitation goes on a commercial certificate issued without an instrument rating?
a: The certificate carries the limitation 'Carrying passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights of more than 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited', per 61.133(b), Part 61, Subpart F, 'Commercial pilot privileges and limitations.' Adding the instrument rating removes it; the limitation can be taken off by submitting the certificate for reissue once the rating is earned.
dup: What exact limitation is placed on a commercial certificate issued without an instrument rating?

concept: Instrument rating required for flight in Class A airspace
q: What is required of the pilot and aircraft to operate in Class A airspace?
a: All operations in Class A are conducted under IFR, so you need an instrument rating, an IFR clearance, an IFR-equipped aircraft, and two-way radio communication, per 91.135, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Operations in Class A airspace,' together with 91.167 through 91.193. Class A runs from 18,000 feet MSL to and including FL600 and an unpressurized Warrior II will never reach it.
dup: What is required to operate in Class A airspace?

concept: Instrument rating required for Special VFR between sunset and sunrise
q: What does 91.157 require of a pilot who wants Special VFR at night?
a: Between sunset and sunrise the pilot must be instrument rated and current, and the aircraft must be equipped for instrument flight, per 91.157(b)(4), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Special VFR weather minimums.' Special VFR in any case requires an ATC clearance, clear of clouds, and at least 1 statute mile flight visibility, and it is never available where the chart says 'NO SVFR.'
dup: What is Special VFR and what does it require?

concept: To act as PIC under IFR you need a current medical certificate or BasicMed with restrictions
q: What medical qualification lets you act as PIC under IFR?
a: A current medical certificate of the appropriate class, or operating under BasicMed with its restrictions, per 61.23, Part 61, Subpart A, 'Medical certificates: Requirement and duration.' BasicMed permits IFR flight but limits you to aircraft with no more than 7 occupant seats and 12,500 pounds maximum certificated takeoff weight, no more than 6 passengers, below 18,000 feet MSL and 250 knots indicated, and never for compensation or hire.
dup: Is BasicMed a medical certificate?

concept: To act as PIC under IFR you need a current instrument rating
q: Besides the rating itself, what recency do you need to act as PIC under IFR?
a: Within the preceding 6 calendar months you must have logged six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems, per 61.57(c), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Recent flight experience: Pilot in command.' Lose it and you have 6 more calendar months to regain it with a safety pilot or instructor; after that it takes an instrument proficiency check.
dup: What must you have done in the preceding 6 calendar months to act as PIC under IFR?

concept: Mandatory IFR report: any unforecast weather conditions
q: Must you report weather to ATC under IFR, and which weather?
a: Yes. You must report any unforecast weather conditions encountered, per 91.183(c), Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications.' That includes unexpected icing, turbulence, thunderstorms or conditions that differ from the forecast you planned against. This report is required at all times, radar contact or not.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: vacating any previously assigned altitude or flight level
q: What must you tell ATC when you leave an assigned altitude under IFR?
a: Report vacating any previously assigned altitude or flight level for a newly assigned altitude or flight level, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports, which applies at all times whether or not you are in radar contact. The standard phrasing is 'Warrior four five bravo leaving six thousand for four thousand.'

concept: Mandatory IFR report: time and altitude or flight level upon reaching a holding fix
q: What do you report when you arrive at a holding fix or clearance limit?
a: The time and altitude or flight level upon reaching a holding fix or the point to which you were cleared, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times, in radar contact or not, because ATC uses it to protect the airspace and plan your onward clearance.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: leaving any assigned holding fix or point
q: What report is required when you leave a holding fix?
a: Report leaving any assigned holding fix or point, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports, required at all times whether or not in radar contact. Together with the report on reaching the fix, it brackets your time in the hold for ATC.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: compulsory reporting points
q: What are compulsory reporting points, and when must you report over them?
a: They are fixes shown on en route charts as solid triangles, and a position report is required over them when you are not in radar contact, per 91.183(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications,' and AIM 5-3-2. Open triangles are on-request reporting points. The report contains identification, position, time, altitude, type of flight plan and ETA for the next fix.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: unable to climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute
q: When must you tell ATC about your climb or descent rate?
a: Whenever you are unable to climb or descend at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times. On a warm day at gross weight a Warrior II can easily fall below 500 feet per minute in the climb through the mid-altitudes, so this report comes up in real life; check the POH climb performance chart before accepting a high altitude.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: executing a missed approach
q: What must you report if you go missed?
a: Report when an approach has been missed, and request clearance for specific action, for example another approach or clearance to the alternate, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times, in radar contact or not.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: change in average true airspeed at cruise of 5 percent or 10 knots
q: When does a change in true airspeed have to be reported to ATC?
a: When the average true airspeed at cruising altitude varies by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from that filed in the flight plan, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. It is required at all times. For a Warrior II filed at 110 knots true, 10 knots is the greater figure, so a sustained change of 10 knots or more is reportable.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: loss of navigation capability
q: What must you report if navigation or communication equipment fails under IFR?
a: You must report any loss of VOR, TACAN, ADF, low frequency navigation receiver capability, GPS anomalies while using installed IFR-certified GPS, complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability, or impairment of air-ground communications, per 91.187, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports.' Include aircraft identification, the equipment affected, the degree of impairment, and the assistance you want.

concept: Mandatory IFR report: any information relating to the safety of flight
q: Is there a catch-all IFR reporting item?
a: Yes. You must report any information relating to the safety of flight, per 91.183(c), Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications.' If something is happening that ATC would want to know about to keep you or anyone else safe, tell them; this is the clause that covers everything the specific items do not.

concept: Which IFR reports are required only when not in radar contact
q: Which IFR reports are required only when you are not in radar contact?
a: Three: leaving the final approach fix or outer marker inbound on final approach; a corrected estimate whenever a previously submitted estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes; and position reports over compulsory reporting points, per AIM 5-3-3, Reports. In the North Atlantic the corrected estimate threshold is 3 minutes. Everything else on the list is required at all times.

concept: AIM 5-3-3 as the source for IFR position and additional reports
q: Where do you look up the full list of required IFR reports?
a: AIM paragraph 5-3-3, 'Reports,' in Chapter 5, En Route Procedures, which splits them into reports required at all times and reports required only when not in radar contact. The regulatory hooks are 91.183, Part 91, Subpart B, 'IFR communications,' and 91.187, 'Operation under IFR in controlled airspace: Malfunction reports.'

concept: 91.167 IFR fuel requirements rule
q: Which regulation sets IFR fuel requirements, and what is its official title?
a: 14 CFR 91.167, Part 91, Subpart B, titled 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions.' In plain English, no person may operate a civil aircraft in IFR conditions unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first airport of intended landing, then to the most distant alternate if one is required, and then for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed. Helicopters use 30 minutes instead of 45.

concept: IFR fuel: fuel from departure to the first airport of intended landing
q: What is the first of the three IFR fuel legs?
a: Enough fuel to complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather, per 91.167(a)(1), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions.' That means the fuel to fly the filed route and the expected approach, not the great circle distance.

concept: IFR fuel: fuel from the destination to the most distant alternate
q: What is the second IFR fuel leg, and when does it apply?
a: Fuel to fly from that airport to the most distant alternate airport listed in the flight plan, per 91.167(a)(2), Part 91, Subpart B. It applies only if an alternate is required or filed. If you file two alternates you must carry fuel to reach the farther one.

concept: IFR fuel: plus 45 minutes at normal cruising speed
q: What is the IFR fuel reserve, and how is it calculated?
a: 45 minutes at normal cruising speed, after the destination and any alternate, per 91.167(a)(3), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions.' It is a time reserve computed at normal cruise fuel flow and altitude, not a fixed gallon figure, and unlike the VFR rule it is 45 minutes day or night.

concept: The alternate fuel leg applies only if an alternate is required: the 1-2-3 rule
q: When is an IFR alternate not required?
a: When the destination has a standard instrument approach procedure and, for at least 1 hour before through 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the forecast ceiling is at least 2,000 feet above airport elevation and visibility at least 3 statute miles, per 91.167(b), Part 91, Subpart B. That is the 1-2-3 rule. Alternate airport weather minimums themselves are in 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'

concept: Applying 91.167 to the PA-28-161 Warrior II
q: How do you turn the 91.167 fuel rule into gallons in your Warrior II?
a: Take the planned cruise fuel flow from the POH cruise performance tables, typically around 8 to 9 gallons per hour for a 160 horsepower Lycoming O-320 at a normal cruise power setting, and multiply by the time to destination, plus time to the alternate if required, plus 0.75 hour for the 45-minute reserve. Add taxi, runup, climb and any approach allowance, then compare against usable fuel, which is 48 gallons on most Warrior IIs; confirm your airplane's usable fuel and fuel flow against the POH.

concept: Required personal documents a pilot must carry
q: What personal documents must you have with you to exercise your pilot privileges?
a: Your pilot certificate, your medical certificate or BasicMed documentation, and an acceptable photo identification, per 61.3, Part 61, Subpart A, 'Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations.' For flight outside the United States add a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit. All must be in your physical or electronic possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, and presented on request to the FAA, NTSB, TSA or any federal, state or local law enforcement officer.
dup: What three documents must you have on your person to act as pilot in command?

concept: Personal document: pilot certificate
q: What does the regulation say about carrying your pilot certificate?
a: No person may act as pilot in command unless that person has a valid pilot certificate in that person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, per 61.3(a), Part 61, Subpart A. A plastic or paper FAA certificate does not expire, but it must be the current one for the privileges exercised, and a temporary certificate is valid only until the expiry date printed on it.

concept: Personal document: medical certificate or BasicMed
q: What medical documentation must you carry, and what does BasicMed require you to have?
a: A medical certificate of the appropriate class in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, per 61.3(c), Part 61, Subpart A, 'Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations.' Under BasicMed you instead carry your logbook with the course completion endorsement and have the completed Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist, FAA Form 8700-2, available. Commercial pilots flying for compensation or hire need at least a second class medical; BasicMed will not do.
dup: Is BasicMed a medical certificate?

concept: Personal document: authorized photo identification
q: What counts as acceptable photo identification under 61.3?
a: A government-issued photo ID: a driver's license issued by a state, the District of Columbia or a United States territory; a United States or foreign passport; a government identification card issued by a federal, state, county or municipal body; an armed forces identification card; or an official credential of a United States armed forces member or employee, per 61.3(a)(2), Part 61, Subpart A.
dup: What counts as acceptable photo identification for 61.3?

concept: Personal document: radio operator permit for flight outside the United States
q: When do you personally need a radio operator permit?
a: For flight outside the United States, where you need an FCC Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit, issued under 47 CFR Part 13 and valid for the holder's lifetime. It is not required for purely domestic flights within the United States. The aircraft separately needs an FCC radio station license for international operation.

concept: ARROW mnemonic and the regulations behind it
q: What does ARROW stand for, and which rules require those documents?
a: A for Airworthiness certificate, R for Registration certificate, R for Radio station license (international flights only), O for Operating limitations and information, W for Weight and balance data. The airworthiness and registration certificates are required by 91.203, Part 91, Subpart C, 'Civil aircraft: Certifications required'; the operating limitations and markings by 91.9, 'Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements,' with the flight manual content set by 21.5; the radio station license by the FCC under 47 CFR Part 87.
dup: What does ARROW stand for, and what requires those documents to be aboard?

concept: ARROW A: airworthiness certificate
q: Does the airworthiness certificate expire, and where must it be kept?
a: A standard airworthiness certificate has no expiry date; it stays valid as long as the aircraft is maintained in accordance with Parts 21, 43 and 91 and the registration remains effective, per 21.181 and 91.203. It must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so that it is legible to passengers or crew, per 91.203(b). In a Warrior II that means visible in the baggage area window or on the door post.
dup: Does the airworthiness certificate expire, and what keeps it valid?

concept: ARROW R: registration certificate
q: How long is an aircraft registration certificate valid, and what must be aboard?
a: The original or a copy of the Certificate of Aircraft Registration, FAA Form 8050-3, must be aboard, per 91.203(a)(2), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Civil aircraft: Certifications required.' Registration is now issued for 7 years and must be renewed before it expires; renewal may be done online. The registration also lapses on sale, destruction, scrapping, cancellation, or registration in a foreign country.
dup: How long is an aircraft registration certificate valid?

concept: ARROW R: radio station license for international flights
q: When does the airplane itself need a radio station license?
a: Only for flight outside the United States or when communicating with foreign stations. The FCC Aircraft Radio Station License is issued under 47 CFR Part 87, is valid for 10 years, and is not an FAA document. A domestic Warrior II flying only within the United States does not need one.
dup: When is an FCC radio station license required?

concept: ARROW O: operating limitations and information in the AFM
q: What counts as the operating limitations, and where do you find them?
a: The FAA-approved Airplane Flight Manual or the approved POH, together with placards, instrument markings and any required listings, per 91.9, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements,' with flight manual content prescribed by 21.5. For a 1981 PA-28-161 Warrior II the approved POH with its weight and balance supplements and any STC supplements serves as the AFM and must be in the airplane.
dup: What counts as the operating limitations, and where do you find them?

concept: ARROW W: weight and balance data specific to the aircraft
q: What weight and balance data must be in the airplane, and who produces it?
a: The current, aircraft-specific weight and balance report showing the empty weight, empty weight center of gravity and the equipment list, as amended by every mechanic who adds, removes or relocates equipment, and recorded under 43.9. It is required aboard as part of the operating limitations and information under 91.9. Use the actual sheet for your Warrior II's tail number, never a generic POH sample.
dup: What weight and balance data must be in the airplane, and who produces it?

concept: IM SAFE preflight self-assessment, 91.17 and AIM 8-1-1
q: What is the IM SAFE checklist, and what does each letter stand for?
a: A personal fitness-for-flight self-assessment: I for Illness, M for Medication, S for Stress, A for Alcohol, F for Fatigue, E for Emotion and Eating. It is the practical expression of 91.17, Part 91, Subpart A, 'Alcohol or drugs,' and 61.53, 'Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency,' and it is described in AIM 8-1-1, Fitness for Flight. If any item is a yes, you do not fly.

concept: IM SAFE I: Illness
q: What does the I in IM SAFE ask you, and what rule backs it up?
a: Illness. Are you sick, and would the symptoms, even a head cold, affect your ability to fly safely? A cold blocks the eustachian tubes and can cause a painful or damaging ear or sinus block on descent. 61.53, Part 61, Subpart A, 'Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency,' forbids acting as a required crewmember while you know of any medical condition that would make you unable to meet the requirements for your medical certificate.

concept: IM SAFE M: Medication
q: What does the M in IM SAFE ask, and where do you check a drug?
a: Medication. Are you taking any prescription or over-the-counter drug, and is it or the underlying condition disqualifying? 91.17(a)(3) forbids acting as a crewmember while using any drug that affects your faculties in a way contrary to safety. Many antihistamines and sleep aids are grounding. Check the FAA's published list of Do Not Issue and Do Not Fly medications or ask an aviation medical examiner.

concept: IM SAFE S: Stress
q: What does the S in IM SAFE ask of you?
a: Stress. Are you under psychological pressure from work, money, family or health that will occupy your attention in the cockpit? Stress narrows attention and degrades decision making and short-term memory, which is exactly what you need on a commercial checkride or a single-pilot IFR approach. AIM 8-1-1 treats stress as a fitness item on a par with illness.

concept: IM SAFE A: Alcohol
q: What does the A in IM SAFE ask, and what is the legal limit?
a: Alcohol. Under 91.17, Part 91, Subpart A, 'Alcohol or drugs,' no person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember within 8 hours after consuming any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, or with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater. Eight hours is the legal floor, not a physiological safe margin, and hangover effects persist well beyond it.

concept: 91.17 hard numbers: 8 hours, 0.04 percent, refusal to submit to a test
q: State the exact numbers and penalties in 91.17.
a: 8 hours bottle to throttle and a blood alcohol concentration below 0.04 percent, and no acting as a crewmember while under the influence of alcohol or any drug affecting your faculties, per 91.17(a), Part 91, Subpart A, 'Alcohol or drugs.' Refusing a test requested by a law enforcement officer, or refusing to furnish the results, is itself grounds for denial of an application for up to 1 year or for suspension or revocation of your certificate under 91.17(c) and (d).

concept: IM SAFE F: Fatigue
q: What does the F in IM SAFE ask, and why is fatigue so dangerous?
a: Fatigue. Are you tired, and have you had proper rest? Fatigue is insidious because it degrades judgment and attention before the pilot notices, and the fatigued pilot is the worst judge of his own state. It is a leading factor in night and long cross-country accidents, and AIM 8-1-1 treats it as a go or no-go item. Acute fatigue is cured by rest; chronic fatigue is not.

concept: IM SAFE E: Emotion and Eating
q: What does the final E in IM SAFE cover?
a: Emotion and Eating. Emotion asks whether you are upset, angry or grieving, any of which captures attention and degrades judgment. Eating asks whether you are properly nourished and hydrated, because low blood sugar and dehydration cause headache, slow thinking and poor decisions, and they build up through a long day of commercial flying. Carry water and food on any flight of length.

concept: PAVE preflight risk checklist
q: What is the PAVE checklist, and what does each letter cover?
a: A preflight risk assessment covering the four risk areas of any flight: P for Pilot, A for Aircraft, V for enVironment, E for External pressures. You run it before the flight to identify hazards and set a personal go or no-go, and the FAA Risk Management Handbook and AC 60-22, Aeronautical Decision Making, describe how to score and mitigate each element.

concept: PAVE P: Pilot
q: What do you assess under the P of PAVE?
a: The Pilot. Your fitness and your qualifications: run IM SAFE for illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue and emotion or eating, then check currency and proficiency, recent experience in type, night and instrument currency, and whether your personal minimums cover the conditions. Current is not the same as proficient.

concept: PAVE A: Aircraft
q: What do you assess under the A of PAVE?
a: The Aircraft. Is it airworthy and legal: ARROW documents aboard, AV1ATES inspections current, no inoperative equipment outside 91.213, fuel and oil adequate, weight and balance within limits, and performance adequate for the runway, density altitude and terrain. For a Warrior II with 160 horsepower, the takeoff and climb charts in the POH are the deciding document on a hot day at a short strip.

concept: PAVE V: enVironment
q: What do you assess under the V of PAVE?
a: The enVironment. Weather, terrain, airspace, airport conditions, runway surface and length, lighting, day or night, icing and thunderstorms, density altitude, and the condition of navigation aids and TFRs along the route. It is the widest of the four categories and the one that changes while you are airborne, so it needs reassessment in flight, not just before departure.

concept: PAVE E: External pressures
q: What do you assess under the E of PAVE, and why does it matter commercially?
a: External pressures. The forces pushing you to complete the flight: a paying passenger, a schedule, a checkride slot, getting home, the cost of a night in a hotel. As a commercial pilot these grow sharply, and they drive get-there-itis and continued VFR into instrument conditions. The defense is to set an alternate plan and a decision point before departure so the pressure meets a prior commitment.

concept: DECIDE model for decision making and risk management
q: What is the DECIDE model, and what does each letter stand for?
a: A six-step continuous decision loop: D for Detect a change has occurred, E for Estimate the need to counter the change, C for Choose a desirable outcome, I for Identify actions to control the change, D for Do take the necessary action, E for Evaluate the effect of the action. It is described in the FAA Risk Management Handbook and AC 60-22, Aeronautical Decision Making, and it repeats until the situation is resolved.

concept: DECIDE D: Detect a change has occurred
q: What is the first step of DECIDE, and why is it the one pilots miss?
a: Detect that a change has occurred. You cannot act on a problem you have not noticed, and most accident chains start with a cue that was present and unobserved, such as a slowly falling oil pressure, a ceiling coming down, or a fuel burn running ahead of plan. The defense is a deliberate scan and periodic cross-check of instruments, weather and fuel against the plan.

concept: DECIDE E: Estimate the need to counter the change
q: What is the second step of DECIDE?
a: Estimate the need to counter or react to the change. You judge how serious it is and whether it actually requires action, how much time you have, and what it threatens. Not every change needs a response, but assuming that it does not is how a minor deviation becomes an emergency.

concept: DECIDE C: Choose what is the desired outcome
q: What is the third step of DECIDE?
a: Choose a desirable outcome for the flight. Before you pick an action you decide what success now looks like, which may no longer be arriving at the planned destination. Setting the outcome first, for example 'a safe landing at a suitable airport within 30 minutes,' keeps the later options honest.

concept: DECIDE I: Identify the solutions
q: What is the fourth step of DECIDE?
a: Identify actions that could successfully control the change. You list the realistic options, for example continue, divert, hold, climb, descend, turn back, or declare an emergency, and weigh each against the outcome you chose. Generating more than one option is the point; a pilot who sees only one option has usually stopped thinking.

concept: DECIDE D: Do the necessary actions
q: What is the fifth step of DECIDE?
a: Do take the necessary action. Commit and fly the chosen option, in the order aviate, navigate, communicate. Deciding and then not acting, or acting half way, is the common failure: a diversion begun late burns the margin that made it the safe choice.

concept: DECIDE E: Evaluate the effects of the actions
q: What is the sixth step of DECIDE, and what happens after it?
a: Evaluate the effect of the action. Did it fix the problem, and did it create a new one? The model is a loop, not a line, so evaluation feeds straight back into detecting the next change. This is also where you check that workload and fuel still support the new plan.

concept: AV1ATES mnemonic for required aircraft maintenance inspections
q: What does AV1ATES stand for, and what inspections must be current to fly?
a: A for Annual every 12 calendar months, V for VOR check every 30 days for IFR, 1 for 100-hour inspection when carrying persons for hire or giving flight instruction for hire, A for Altimeter and static system every 24 calendar months, T for Transponder every 24 calendar months, E for ELT every 12 calendar months, S for Static system every 24 calendar months. The altimeter and static items come from the same inspection under 91.411, which is why the mnemonic lists them twice.
dup: What inspections must be current for the airplane to be legal to fly?

concept: AV1ATES A: annual inspection every 12 calendar months, 91.409
q: What is the annual inspection requirement, and who may sign it off?
a: No person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 calendar months, it has had an annual inspection and been approved for return to service, per 91.409(a), Part 91, Subpart E, 'Inspections.' It must be done by an airframe and powerplant mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization, a certificated repair station, or the manufacturer. Calendar month means it is good to the last day of the twelfth month.
dup: What is the annual inspection requirement, and who may perform it?

concept: AV1ATES V: VOR check every 30 days, 91.171
q: How recently must a VOR have been checked, and for what kind of flying?
a: Within the preceding 30 days before operating under IFR using that VOR, per 91.171(a), Part 91, Subpart C, 'VOR equipment check for IFR operations.' It is 30 days, not a calendar month. There is no VOR check requirement for VFR flight, although a VOR you intend to navigate by should still be verified.

concept: AV1ATES 1: 100-hour inspection, 91.409, required if flying for hire
q: When is a 100-hour inspection required, and by how much may it be exceeded?
a: When the aircraft carries any person other than a crewmember for hire, or is given for flight instruction for hire, per 91.409(b), Part 91, Subpart E, 'Inspections.' It may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours, and only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done; any excess is subtracted from the next 100-hour interval. An annual may substitute for a 100-hour, but a 100-hour may not substitute for an annual.
dup: When is a 100-hour inspection required?

concept: AV1ATES A: altimeter and static system test every 24 calendar months, 91.411
q: What is the altimeter and altitude reporting inspection requirement?
a: For IFR flight in controlled airspace, the static pressure system, each altimeter instrument and the automatic pressure altitude reporting system must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months, per 91.411, Part 91, Subpart E, 'Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections.' The work must be done by the manufacturer, a certificated repair station, or, for the static system only, a certificated mechanic with an airframe rating.
dup: What is the altimeter, static system and altitude reporting inspection requirement?

concept: AV1ATES T: transponder test every 24 calendar months, 91.413
q: What is the transponder inspection requirement, and does it apply to VFR flight?
a: No person may use an ATC transponder unless it has been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months, per 91.413, Part 91, Subpart E, 'ATC transponder tests and inspections.' It applies whenever the transponder is used, VFR or IFR, so an out-of-date transponder cannot legally be switched on in flight. The test is done by a repair station, the manufacturer, or a holder of a continuous airworthiness maintenance program.
