concept: AV1ATES E: ELT inspection every 12 calendar months, 91.207
q: How often must the emergency locator transmitter be inspected, and what does the inspection cover?
a: Every 12 calendar months, per 91.207(d), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Emergency locator transmitters.' The inspection checks proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and the absence of radiated energy. The inspection date is recorded in the maintenance record and the ELT must be attached to the airplane in the manner the rule prescribes.
dup: How often must an emergency locator transmitter be inspected?

concept: ELT battery replacement: after more than 1 hour of cumulative use or when 50 percent of useful life has expired
q: When must the ELT battery be replaced or recharged?
a: When the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life, or for a rechargeable battery 50 percent of its useful charge life, has expired, per 91.207(c), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Emergency locator transmitters.' The new expiration date must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the aircraft maintenance record.
dup: When must an ELT battery be replaced or recharged?

concept: AV1ATES S: static system test every 24 calendar months, 91.411
q: Why does the static system appear twice in AV1ATES, and what is its interval?
a: Because the static pressure system, the altimeter and the altitude reporting equipment are all covered by the same 24 calendar month test under 91.411, Part 91, Subpart E. The mnemonic lists the A and the S separately only as a memory aid. If the static system is opened and closed for maintenance, the system must be tested again before IFR flight.

concept: Confirmation of airworthiness is the responsibility of the pilot in command
q: Who is responsible for determining that the airplane is airworthy for today's flight?
a: The pilot in command, per 91.7(b), Part 91, Subpart A, 'Civil aircraft airworthiness,' which also requires the PIC to discontinue the flight when an unairworthy condition occurs. The owner or operator is separately responsible for keeping the aircraft in airworthy condition and for compliance with airworthiness directives and required inspections under 91.403. Airworthy means it conforms to its type certificate and is in condition for safe operation.
dup: Who is responsible for keeping an aircraft airworthy, and who decides it is airworthy today?

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES: minimum required equipment for day VFR flight, 91.205(b)
q: What does A TOMATO FLAMES stand for, and which rule is it?
a: The day VFR equipment list of 91.205(b), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Instrument and equipment requirements': A Altimeter, T Tachometer for each engine, O Oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, M Manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine, A Airspeed indicator, T Temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine, O Oil pressure gauge for each engine using a pressure system, F Fuel quantity gauge for each tank, L Landing gear position indicator, A Anticollision lights, M Magnetic direction indicator, E ELT, S Safety belts and shoulder harnesses. Add approved flotation gear for flight for hire beyond gliding distance of shore.
dup: What instruments and equipment must be installed and working for VFR day flight?

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES A: altimeter
q: What altimeter is required for day VFR, and how does it work?
a: An altimeter is required by 91.205(b)(2), Part 91, Subpart C. For day VFR it need only be an altimeter; the sensitive, barometrically adjustable altimeter is an IFR item under 91.205(d). It is an aneroid barometer: sealed wafers expand as static pressure falls, and the linkage drives the pointers against the setting in the Kollsman window.
dup: How does an altimeter work?

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES T: tachometer for each engine
q: What does the day VFR list require about the tachometer?
a: A tachometer for each engine, per 91.205(b)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. In a fixed-pitch Warrior II the tachometer is your power instrument, because with no constant speed propeller RPM is the direct measure of power set; most also carry a recording hour meter used to track the 100-hour and oil change intervals. Confirm the green arc and redline for your airplane against the POH.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES O: oil temperature indicator
q: Which engines need an oil temperature gauge for day VFR?
a: An oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, per 91.205(b)(10), Part 91, Subpart C. A Warrior II's Lycoming O-320 is air-cooled, so the oil temperature gauge is required equipment, not an option. Oil carries away a large share of the engine's heat, so oil temperature is your early indicator of a cooling or lubrication problem.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES M: manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine
q: When is a manifold pressure gauge required for day VFR?
a: Only for each altitude engine, that is a supercharged or turbocharged engine, per 91.205(b)(5), Part 91, Subpart C. A normally aspirated, carbureted Lycoming O-320 in a Warrior II is not an altitude engine, so no manifold pressure gauge is required; in practice airplanes with constant speed propellers carry one anyway to set power.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES A: airspeed indicator
q: What airspeed instrument is required for day VFR?
a: An airspeed indicator, per 91.205(b)(1), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements.' It is a differential pressure gauge comparing pitot ram air pressure against static pressure. Its color markings, the white and green arcs and the yellow arc and red line, are part of the operating limitations required by 91.9.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES T: temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine
q: Does your Warrior II need a coolant temperature gauge?
a: No. 91.205(b)(9), Part 91, Subpart C, requires a temperature gauge only for each liquid-cooled engine. The Lycoming O-320 in a PA-28-161 is a horizontally opposed, air-cooled engine: cooling air enters the front cowl inlets, is forced down between the cylinder fins by baffles and pressure differential, and exits the cowl outlet, so there is no coolant to measure.
dup: What does it mean that an engine is horizontally opposed and air cooled?

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES O: oil pressure gauge for each engine
q: What does the day VFR list require about oil pressure?
a: An oil pressure gauge for each engine using a pressure oil system, per 91.205(b)(4), Part 91, Subpart C. The Warrior II's wet sump Lycoming is a pressure system, so the gauge is required. Oil pressure should come up within about 30 seconds of start, or sooner in warm weather; if it does not, shut down. Confirm the green arc limits against the POH.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES F: fuel quantity gauge for each tank
q: What does 91.205 require for fuel indication?
a: A fuel gauge indicating the quantity of usable fuel in each tank, per 91.205(b)(9), Part 91, Subpart C. Note it indicates usable fuel, and it is only required by certification standards to read accurately at empty. In a Warrior II that means you plan on time and known fuel flow, dip or visually check the two wing tanks before flight, and treat the gauges as a cross-check.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES L: landing gear position lights
q: When is a landing gear position indicator required?
a: Only if the airplane has retractable landing gear, per 91.205(b)(8), Part 91, Subpart C. The usual arrangement is three green lights for down and locked and a red or amber light in transit, driven by squat and uplock switches. A Warrior II has fixed tricycle gear, so this item does not apply to your airplane.
dup: How is retractable gear operated, and what tells you it is down?

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES A: anticollision lights for aircraft certificated after March 11, 1996
q: Which airplanes must have an anticollision light system, and must yours be on?
a: An approved anticollision light system is required equipment for small civil airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, per 91.205(b)(11), Part 91, Subpart C. A 1981 Warrior II was certificated before that date, so the system is not required equipment; but under 91.209(b), if an anticollision light system is installed, it must be on for all operations unless the pilot in command determines in the interest of safety that it should be turned off, for example in cloud or on the ramp around people.
dup: Which items on the VFR day list only apply to some airplanes?

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES M: magnetic compass
q: What does 91.205 call the compass, and what must accompany it?
a: A magnetic direction indicator, per 91.205(b)(3), Part 91, Subpart C, which in a Warrior II is the wet magnetic compass on the windshield post. It must be accompanied by a current deviation correction card showing the compass headings for at least every 30 degrees, and it must be legible and in place; the compass is also the only heading source that needs no electrical or vacuum power.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES E: emergency locator transmitter
q: Is an ELT required for day VFR, and may you ever fly without one?
a: Yes, an emergency locator transmitter meeting 91.207 is required by 91.205(b)(13), Part 91, Subpart C. An aircraft may be operated without an ELT for up to 90 days while the unit is removed for inspection, repair, modification or replacement, provided the aircraft records show the removal date and a placard reading 'ELT not installed' is placed in view of the pilot. Other exceptions in 91.207(f) cover ferry, training within 50 nautical miles and certain single-seat aircraft.

concept: A TOMATO FLAMES S: safety belts and shoulder harnesses
q: What does 91.205 require for belts and harnesses, and when must they be worn?
a: An approved safety belt for each occupant 2 years of age or older, and a shoulder harness for each front seat on airplanes manufactured after July 18, 1978, per 91.205(b)(12) and (b)(14), Part 91, Subpart C. Under 91.107 the pilot must brief occupants to fasten belts, and each occupant must have the belt fastened for taxi, takeoff and landing; a shoulder harness, if installed, must be worn for takeoff and landing unless the person cannot perform required duties with it on.

concept: Night VFR equipment is all of the day VFR equipment plus FLAPS
q: What is the rule for building the night VFR equipment list?
a: Everything required for day VFR under 91.205(b) plus the night items of 91.205(c), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements.' The night additions are remembered as FLAPS: Fuses, Landing light if for hire, Anticollision lights, Position lights, Source of electrical power.
dup: What must be added to the VFR day equipment for flight at night?

concept: FLAPS mnemonic for night VFR equipment, 91.205(c)
q: What does FLAPS stand for, and which regulation is it?
a: The night VFR additions of 91.205(c), Part 91, Subpart C: F for Fuses, a spare set or three spare fuses of each kind required and accessible in flight; L for Landing light, required only if the aircraft is operated for hire; A for Anticollision light system; P for Position lights, the navigation lights; S for Source of electrical energy adequate for all installed electrical and radio equipment.
dup: What equipment is required for night VFR flight, and what mnemonic covers it?

concept: FLAPS F: spare fuses
q: What does the fuse requirement actually say, and what if the airplane has circuit breakers?
a: One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, accessible to the pilot in flight, per 91.205(c)(5), Part 91, Subpart C. If the airplane uses resettable circuit breakers instead of fuses, as most Warrior IIs do, there is nothing to carry and the requirement is satisfied by the breakers. Check which your airplane has; some Piper panels mix the two.
dup: Why are spare fuses required for night flight, and what if the aircraft has circuit breakers?

concept: FLAPS L: landing light if for hire
q: Is a landing light legally required at night?
a: Only if the aircraft is operated for hire, per 91.205(c)(4), Part 91, Subpart C. A privately operated Warrior II may legally fly at night with the landing light inoperative, provided it is deactivated or removed and placarded under 91.213(d). Flying a night landing without one is legal and unwise, and as a commercial pilot carrying passengers for hire it is required.
dup: Is a landing light legally required for night flight?

concept: FLAPS A: anticollision light
q: What are the rules for anticollision lights at night?
a: An approved aviation red or aviation white anticollision light system is required for night VFR under 91.205(c)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. Under 91.209(b), if such a system is installed it must be on for all operations, day or night, unless the pilot in command determines in the interest of safety that it should be off, such as in cloud where strobe reflection is disorienting, or with people near the airplane.
dup: What are the rules for anticollision lights?

concept: FLAPS P: position lights
q: When must position lights be on, and what period governs it?
a: From sunset to sunrise, per 91.209(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Aircraft lights.' No person may operate an aircraft during that period, or in Alaska during the period a prominent unlighted object cannot be seen from 3 statute miles or the sun is more than 6 degrees below the horizon, unless it has lighted position lights, and no person may park or move it in a night operating area unless it is lighted or marked. Note this is sunset to sunrise, a different period from the 61.1 definition of night used for logging.
dup: What period governs when position lights must be on?

concept: FLAPS S: source of electrical power
q: What does the source of power item require at night?
a: An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment, per 91.205(c)(2), Part 91, Subpart C. In a Warrior II that is the engine-driven alternator with the battery as the reserve. If the alternator fails at night, shed load immediately to lights and one radio; expect well under an hour of useful battery time, and confirm the POH electrical failure checklist.

concept: GRABCARD: minimum equipment for IFR flight is day VFR plus FLAPS at night plus 91.205(d)
q: What does GRABCARD stand for, and what else must be aboard for IFR?
a: The IFR additions of 91.205(d), Part 91, Subpart C: G Generator or alternator, R Radios, A Altimeter that is sensitive and adjustable, B Ball, C Clock, A Attitude indicator, R Rate of turn indicator, D Directional gyro. They are on top of everything required for day VFR, plus the FLAPS night items if the flight is at night. Above FL240, if VOR is required for the route, DME or a suitable RNAV system is also required by 91.205(e).
dup: What equipment must be added on top of the VFR lists to fly IFR?

concept: GRABCARD G: generator or alternator
q: What does the G of GRABCARD require, and how does it differ from a generator?
a: A generator or alternator of adequate capacity, per 91.205(d)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. An alternator produces alternating current rectified to direct current, is lighter, and produces useful output at low RPM, including at idle on the ground; a generator is heavier and produces little below about 1,200 RPM. A Warrior II has a belt-driven alternator with a voltage regulator and an over-voltage relay.
dup: What is the difference between an alternator and a generator?

concept: GRABCARD R: radios, two-way communication and navigation
q: What does the R of GRABCARD require?
a: Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route to be flown, per 91.205(d)(2), Part 91, Subpart C. Suitable means appropriate to the ground facilities or the satellite navigation to be used: for a Warrior II with a panel-mount VOR and an IFR-approved GPS, that means the equipment is installed, operational, and approved for the approaches and routes you have filed.

concept: GRABCARD A: sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure
q: What kind of altimeter does IFR flight require?
a: A sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure, per 91.205(d)(1), Part 91, Subpart C. Sensitive means it reads in 20-foot increments over a 1,000-foot per revolution scale, and the Kollsman window must be settable so you can apply the current altimeter setting. It must also have been tested with the static system within the preceding 24 calendar months under 91.411.

concept: GRABCARD B: ball, the slip-skid indicator
q: What does the B of GRABCARD require, and what does the instrument tell you?
a: A slip-skid indicator, the inclinometer ball, per 91.205(d)(5), Part 91, Subpart C. It shows whether the airplane is in coordinated flight: ball to the inside of the turn means slipping, too little rate for the bank, and ball to the outside means skidding, too much rate for the bank. Step on the ball to correct. It needs no power, and in a Warrior II it is built into the turn coordinator.

concept: GRABCARD C: clock showing hours, minutes and seconds
q: What are the exact requirements for the IFR clock?
a: A clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds, with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation, per 91.205(d)(6), Part 91, Subpart C. It must be installed in the aircraft; a wristwatch or a phone does not satisfy the rule. It is needed for timed approaches, holding, and estimates, which is why the seconds display is specified.

concept: GRABCARD A: attitude indicator
q: What does the attitude indicator requirement say, and how is it driven in a Warrior II?
a: A gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator, the attitude indicator or artificial horizon, per 91.205(d)(7), Part 91, Subpart C. In a typical Warrior II it is air-driven: the engine-driven vacuum pump draws filtered air across buckets on the gyro rotor to spin it at high speed, and erection mechanism ports keep the gyro upright relative to earth's vertical. Confirm the installation in your airplane against the POH, since many have been retrofitted with electronic displays.
dup: How does a vacuum-driven attitude indicator work?

concept: GRABCARD R: rate of turn indicator
q: What does the R for rate of turn require, and what shows it in your airplane?
a: A gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator, per 91.205(d)(4), Part 91, Subpart C. In a Warrior II this is the electrically driven turn coordinator, whose gyro is canted about 30 degrees so it senses both roll and yaw and shows rate of turn; the little airplane's wingtip on the index marks a standard rate turn of 3 degrees per second, 360 degrees in 2 minutes. It is electric, so a vacuum failure leaves it working.
dup: What does the turn coordinator show, and what powers it?

concept: GRABCARD D: directional gyro or heading indicator
q: What does the D of GRABCARD require, and what are that instrument's errors?
a: A gyroscopic direction indicator, the directional gyro or an equivalent such as a slaved HSI, per 91.205(d)(8), Part 91, Subpart C. A non-slaved directional gyro has no north-seeking ability, so it must be set from the magnetic compass in straight and level unaccelerated flight, and it precesses from bearing friction and earth rotation, typically needing realignment about every 15 minutes. It also has mechanical tumble limits on older units.
dup: What are the errors and limits of a directional gyro?

concept: NW KRAFT: preflight information required, 91.103
q: What does NW KRAFT stand for, and which regulation requires it?
a: The preflight action of 91.103, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action': N NOTAMs, W Weather reports and forecasts, K Known traffic delays advised by ATC, R Runway lengths at airports of intended use, A Alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed as planned, F Fuel requirements, T Takeoff and landing distance data. The rule begins by requiring the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight.
dup: What preflight information are you required to gather before a flight?

concept: NW KRAFT N: NOTAMs
q: Are NOTAMs part of the required preflight action, and which ones matter?
a: Yes, they fall under all available information concerning that flight in 91.103, Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' Check NOTAMs for departure, destination and alternate airports, for navigation aids and GPS outages along the route, and for temporary flight restrictions. Get them from an official source such as the FAA NOTAM search or an approved briefing provider, and remember a TFR can be issued after you depart.

concept: NW KRAFT W: weather reports and forecasts
q: What weather must you obtain before a flight under 91.103?
a: Weather reports and forecasts for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' That means the current and forecast conditions at departure, en route, destination and alternates: METARs, TAFs, area forecasts or graphical forecasts, winds aloft, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, PIREPs and icing and turbulence products, all from a source approved for preflight briefing.

concept: NW KRAFT K: known traffic delays
q: What does the known traffic delays item require?
a: Any known traffic delays of which the pilot in command has been advised by ATC, for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' Delays matter because holding burns the fuel you planned as reserve, which is why this item sits next to the fuel requirement in the same paragraph.

concept: NW KRAFT R: runway lengths at airports of intended use
q: Which part of the preflight action rule applies to every single flight?
a: Runway lengths at airports of intended use, and takeoff and landing distance data, per 91.103(b), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' Unlike the weather, fuel, alternatives and delays items, these apply to every flight including a trip around the pattern. Runway length comes from the Chart Supplement or an approved source, and must be compared against the POH distance for the day's weight, wind, surface and density altitude.
dup: Which parts of the preflight action rule apply to every flight?

concept: NW KRAFT A: alternatives available
q: What does the alternatives item of 91.103 require you to think about?
a: Alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' This is more than an IFR alternate airport: it is the set of diversion fields, routes and turnback points you identified before departure, with their weather, runway lengths, fuel availability and hours. Picking them on the ground is the antidote to deciding under pressure in the air.

concept: NW KRAFT F: fuel requirements
q: What fuel planning does 91.103 require, and what are the minimum reserves?
a: Fuel requirements for the flight, per 91.103(a), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' The legal minimums are in 91.151 for VFR, enough to fly to the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes at normal cruising speed by day or 45 minutes at night, and in 91.167 for IFR, destination plus alternate if required plus 45 minutes. Compute them in gallons from the Warrior II POH cruise fuel flow, and treat the legal minimum as a floor, not a plan.
dup: What are the VFR fuel requirements, and how do they change at night?

concept: NW KRAFT T: takeoff and landing performance data
q: What performance data must you have before every flight?
a: Takeoff and landing distance data from the approved flight manual, or other reliable data for an aircraft without one, per 91.103(b), Part 91, Subpart B, 'Preflight action.' For the Warrior II use the POH takeoff and landing distance charts for the day's weight, pressure altitude, temperature, wind and runway surface, then add a margin, because the book numbers were flown by a test pilot in a new airplane on a dry paved runway.

concept: The 30-day VOR check requirement, 91.171
q: What does 91.171 require before you use a VOR under IFR?
a: The VOR equipment must have been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and found to be within the permitted bearing tolerance, per 91.171(a), Part 91, Subpart C, 'VOR equipment check for IFR operations.' It is 30 days, not a calendar month, and it applies to IFR operations only. The check may be made by the pilot; no mechanic is needed except for the repair station method.
dup: How often must a VOR be checked, and does that apply to VFR flying?

concept: The six ways to check a VOR, with tolerances
q: Name the six ways to check VOR accuracy and the tolerance of each.
a: VOT plus or minus 4 degrees; certificated repair station radiated test signal plus or minus 4 degrees; designated VOR ground checkpoint plus or minus 4 degrees; designated VOR airborne checkpoint plus or minus 6 degrees; dual VOR cross-check within 4 degrees of each other; and an airborne check over a prominent ground landmark on a selected radial at least 20 nautical miles from the VOR, plus or minus 6 degrees. All are in 91.171, Part 91, Subpart C, 'VOR equipment check for IFR operations.' Remember ground 4, air 6.
dup: What are the six ways of checking VOR accuracy, and what is the tolerance of each?

concept: VOT check, plus or minus 4 degrees
q: How do you use a VOT, and what tolerance applies?
a: Tune the VOT frequency published in the Chart Supplement and centre the course deviation indicator: it must read 0 degrees with a FROM flag, or 180 degrees with a TO flag, within plus or minus 4 degrees, per 91.171(b)(1), Part 91, Subpart C. The memory aid is 'Cessna 182' for 180 TO and zero FROM. A VOT radiates a test signal only and is used on the ground at the airports that list one.
dup: What is the tolerance for a VOT check, and how is it flown?

concept: Certificated repair station radiated test signal, plus or minus 4 degrees
q: Can a repair station perform a VOR check, and to what tolerance?
a: Yes. A certificated repair station may use a radiated test signal, with a tolerance of plus or minus 4 degrees, per 91.171(b)(2), Part 91, Subpart C, 'VOR equipment check for IFR operations.' The test signal may be radiated only by a repair station holding the appropriate rating, and the repair station makes the required entry; a test signal radiated by anyone else does not satisfy the rule.
dup: Can a repair station perform a VOR check, and to what tolerance?

concept: Designated VOR ground checkpoint, plus or minus 4 degrees
q: What is the tolerance for a VOR ground checkpoint, and where do you find one?
a: Plus or minus 4 degrees, per 91.171(b)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. Ground checkpoints are surveyed spots on an airport surface, listed in the Chart Supplement with the airport entry, giving the exact radial and distance. Taxi the airplane onto the designated spot, tune and identify the VOR, and compare the indicated bearing against the published figure.
dup: What is the tolerance for a VOR ground checkpoint?

concept: Designated VOR airborne checkpoint, plus or minus 6 degrees
q: What is the tolerance for a designated airborne VOR checkpoint?
a: Plus or minus 6 degrees, per 91.171(b)(3), Part 91, Subpart C, 'VOR equipment check for IFR operations.' Airborne checkpoints are published in the Chart Supplement with the radial, distance and altitude to fly, usually over an easily identified landmark. The tolerance is looser than the ground check because of the difficulty of holding position precisely in the air.
dup: What is the tolerance for an airborne VOR checkpoint?

concept: Dual VOR cross-check, within 4 degrees of each other
q: How do you carry out a dual VOR check, and what is the tolerance?
a: With two independent VOR receivers sharing nothing but the antenna, tune both to the same VOR and compare the indicated bearings: the maximum permissible difference between the two is 4 degrees, per 91.171(c), Part 91, Subpart C. It may be done on the ground or in the air. It proves the two agree, not that either is correct, which is why it is only permitted when both are installed.
dup: What is the tolerance for a dual VOR check?

concept: Airborne check over a prominent ground landmark, selected radial at least 20 NM from the VOR, reasonably low altitude, plus or minus 6 degrees
q: If no VOT or published checkpoint is available, how may you check a VOR in the air?
a: Select a VOR radial that passes through a prominent ground point at least 20 nautical miles from the VOR, fly over that point at a reasonably low altitude, and note the bearing: the maximum permissible error is plus or minus 6 degrees, per 91.171(c)(2), Part 91, Subpart C. The 20 nautical miles and the low altitude both exist to reduce the angular error of being slightly off the point.
dup: If no VOT or designated checkpoint is available, how may you check a VOR in the air?

concept: Required VOR check record: date, place, bearing error and signature
q: What must you record after a VOR check, and where does it go?
a: The date, the place, the bearing error, and your signature, per 91.171(d), Part 91, Subpart C, 'VOR equipment check for IFR operations.' The entry goes in the aircraft log or other reliable record; many operators keep a dedicated VOR check log in the airplane. The memory aid is DPES, and no entry means the check did not legally happen.
dup: What must be recorded after a VOR check, and where?

concept: 91.213 decision chain: is the inoperative equipment required by an AD, by the regulations for the type of operation, by VFR-day type certification, or by an operational equipment list
q: Something is inoperative and there is no MEL. What four questions does 91.213(d) make you ask?
a: Is the item required by an airworthiness directive; by the regulations for the kind of flight you are making, such as 91.205; by the VFR-day type certification requirements for the airplane; or by an operational equipment list such as a Kinds of Operations Equipment List in the AFM? This is 91.213(d), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Inoperative instruments and equipment.' A yes to any one of the four grounds the airplane.
dup: Without a MEL, how do you legally fly a small airplane with an inoperative item?

concept: 91.213 yes branch: flight not permitted without a special flight permit
q: If the inoperative item is required equipment, can you still fly, and how?
a: No, not without a special flight permit, a ferry permit, issued under 21.197 and 21.199, Part 21, Subpart H. It is issued for an aircraft that does not currently meet airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight, for purposes such as flying to a base where repairs are to be made, delivering or exporting the aircraft, evacuating from danger, or operating at over maximum certificated takeoff weight for flight beyond normal range. The FAA or an authorized person may impose operating limitations with it.
dup: What is a special flight permit, and when is one used?

concept: 91.213 no branch: the item must be removed, or deactivated and placarded inoperative
q: Once an item passes the 91.213(d) tests, what must be done to it before you fly?
a: It must be removed from the aircraft, the cockpit control placarded, and the maintenance record made under 43.9; or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative', per 91.213(d)(3), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Inoperative instruments and equipment.' Removal or deactivation is maintenance, so if it involves more than placarding it must be done by a person authorized under Part 43 and recorded.
dup: Once the item passes the 91.213(d) tests, what must be done before you fly?

concept: 91.213 no branch: a pilot or mechanic must determine the aircraft is safe to fly
q: Who decides that a flight with an inoperative item is safe to make?
a: A pilot, who must be certificated and appropriately rated, or a repair station or mechanic certificated under Part 43, must determine that the inoperative instrument or equipment does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft, per 91.213(d)(4), Part 91, Subpart C. In practice the pilot in command makes this call on the ramp, and under 91.7(b) remains responsible for determining the aircraft is in condition for safe flight.
dup: Who decides that a flight with an inoperative item is safe to make?

concept: Placard wording INOPERATIVE and the maintenance record entry
q: What exactly goes on the placard, and does the removal have to be recorded?
a: The placard must read 'Inoperative' and be placed at the cockpit control of the affected item, per 91.213(d)(3), Part 91, Subpart C. If the item is removed rather than deactivated, the maintenance record entry required by 43.9, Part 43, 'Content, form, and disposition of maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration records,' must also be made. Placarding alone, with no record, is not enough when removal is the method used.

concept: If the aircraft has a Minimum Equipment List, refer to the MEL guidance
q: How does having a MEL change the inoperative equipment decision?
a: If an approved Minimum Equipment List exists for the aircraft, you must use it and may not use the 91.213(d) route, per 91.213(a), Part 91, Subpart C, 'Inoperative instruments and equipment.' The MEL plus the FAA letter of authorization together become a supplemental type certificate and part of the operating limitations, and the MEL's repair categories A, B, C and D set how long the item may remain inoperative. Most light singles like a Warrior II have no MEL and use 91.213(d).

concept: Required test flight after maintenance affecting flight characteristics, 91.407(b)
q: When is a test flight required after maintenance, and what does 91.407(b) say?
a: 14 CFR 91.407(b), Part 91, Subpart E, 'Operation after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration.' No person may carry any person other than crewmembers in an aircraft that has been maintained, rebuilt or altered in a manner that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics or substantially affected its operation in flight until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate has flown it, made an operational check of the work, and logged the flight in the aircraft records.

concept: Who may fly the 91.407(b) check flight, and what must they log
q: Who may fly the required post-maintenance check flight, and what must be logged?
a: An appropriately rated pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate, who flies the aircraft, makes an operational check of the maintenance performed or alteration made, and logs the flight in the aircraft records, per 91.407(b), Part 91, Subpart E. If the check flight shows the work was not satisfactory, 91.407(c) requires the aircraft to be re-inspected before it is flown again.

concept: No persons other than crewmembers may be carried until the 91.407(b) check flight is complete
q: Your Warrior II has just had major work. Can you take a passenger on the first flight?
a: No. If the work may have appreciably changed the flight characteristics or substantially affected operation in flight, 91.407(b), Part 91, Subpart E, forbids carrying anyone other than crewmembers until the check flight is flown and logged. Required crewmembers may be aboard, so an instructor or safety pilot serving as a crewmember is permitted; a friend along for the ride is not.

concept: DV MONA mnemonic for magnetic compass errors
q: What does DV MONA stand for?
a: The magnetic compass errors: D for Deviation, V for Variation, M for Magnetic dip, O for Oscillation, N for North and South turning errors remembered as UNOS, A for Acceleration errors remembered as ANDS. All of these apply to the wet magnetic compass on the windshield post of a Warrior II, which is your only heading reference with no electrical or vacuum power.

concept: DV MONA D: deviation
q: What is compass deviation, and how is it dealt with?
a: Deviation is the error caused by the airplane's own magnetic fields, from ferrous metal, electrical currents and radios, pulling the compass away from magnetic north. It changes with heading and with what is switched on. A mechanic swings the compass and produces a deviation correction card, required to be in place near the compass, giving the compass heading to steer for each magnetic heading at intervals of not more than 30 degrees. Keep headsets, phones and metal off the glareshield.

concept: DV MONA V: variation
q: What is magnetic variation, and where do you find it?
a: Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north at a given place, caused by the magnetic poles not coinciding with the geographic poles. It is shown on sectional and en route charts by dashed magenta isogonic lines labeled, for example, 11 degrees west, and it changes slowly with time. East is least and west is best: subtract easterly variation from true to get magnetic, add westerly.

concept: DV MONA M: magnetic dip
q: What is magnetic dip and why does it matter?
a: Magnetic dip is the tendency of the compass magnets to align with the earth's magnetic field, which runs into the ground at an increasing angle as you move away from the magnetic equator, pulling the compass card down toward the nearer pole. The card is pendulously mounted so it can tilt, and that tilt is the root cause of both the northerly turning error and the acceleration error. Dip errors are greatest near the poles and nearly absent at the magnetic equator.

concept: DV MONA O: oscillation
q: What is compass oscillation, and what causes it?
a: Oscillation is the erratic swinging of the compass card caused by turbulence, rough control inputs or abrupt maneuvering, which makes the card difficult or impossible to read. The compass bowl is filled with fluid specifically to damp it. The cure is to fly smoothly, wait for the card to settle, and average the swings rather than chase them.

concept: DV MONA N: north and south turning errors
q: What turning error does the compass show, and which way does it go?
a: Northerly turning error: because of magnetic dip, when you roll into a turn from a northerly heading the compass initially indicates a turn in the opposite direction, then lags behind, while from a southerly heading it leads the turn, indicating a greater rate than is actually happening. The errors are greatest on north and south, and essentially zero on east and west, where the compass reads correctly in a turn. This is in the Northern Hemisphere; the senses reverse south of the magnetic equator.

concept: UNOS: undershoot north, overshoot south
q: What is the rule of thumb for rolling out on a northerly or southerly heading using the compass?
a: UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South. Rolling out on a northerly heading, stop the turn before the compass reaches the heading you want; rolling out on a southerly heading, carry the turn past it. The usual lead or lag is roughly the latitude in degrees, so at 40 degrees north you would roll out about 40 degrees early heading north and about 40 degrees late heading south, then let the card settle in wings-level flight.

concept: DV MONA A: acceleration errors
q: What acceleration and deceleration errors does the compass show, and on which headings?
a: On easterly and westerly headings the pendulously mounted, dip-affected card swings when the airplane accelerates or decelerates: acceleration makes the compass indicate a turn toward north, deceleration a turn toward south. The error is greatest on east and west and essentially zero on north and south. In the Southern Hemisphere the senses reverse.

concept: ANDS: accelerate north, decelerate south
q: What does ANDS stand for, and when would it bite you in the Warrior II?
a: ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. Flying east or west, accelerating makes the compass show a turn toward north and decelerating a turn toward south. It bites on a partial panel instrument departure or when leveling off and adding cruise power on an easterly or westerly heading: the compass swings, and a pilot who chases it rolls into a turn he did not intend. Wait for steady speed before reading it.

concept: How the magnetic compass works and the hemisphere caveat
q: How does a magnetic compass work, and which way do the errors run in the Southern Hemisphere?
a: Two small magnets are attached to a float-mounted card suspended in a fluid-filled, sealed bowl; the magnets align with the earth's magnetic field, the fluid damps oscillation and lubricates the pivot, and you read the heading against the lubber line. It needs no electrical or vacuum power, which is why it survives both failures. UNOS and ANDS as stated apply in the Northern Hemisphere; south of the magnetic equator the turning and acceleration errors reverse.
